strengths: The paper addresses a consequential evaluation problem for brain-to-text generation. Testing jointly unseen subjects and unseen stimuli is a meaningful objective with clear relevance to NLP.

The discussion identifies useful distinctions between repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows. The graph illustrations help explain why splitting individual samples can fail to enforce the intended independence.
Coverage of Narratives and ZuCo, two representative decoding models, and four seeds for overlap measurements provides a useful starting point for studying evaluation protocols across modalities.
weaknesses: The supplied algorithms do not enforce the central guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, adds edges for training subjects without excluding held-out texts; Algorithm 2, line 33, adds edges for training tasks without excluding held-out subjects. These expansion steps can reintroduce the prohibited overlap. The prose and pseudocode need reconciliation, supported by explicit checks on the resulting splits.

The reported metrics contain substantive inconsistencies. Table 4 gives EEG2Text ROUGE-1 precision 23.95, recall 23.98, and F-score 25.74, which is incompatible with standard F-score computation under consistent aggregation; Table 3 contains similar cases. Equation 8 also intersects individual signal instances rather than subject identities and leaves division by zero unresolved for held-out subjects absent from training. These issues undermine confidence in both the leakage measurements and benchmark results.

The leakage framing overgeneralizes across evaluation objectives. Sharing subjects across splits can be appropriate when assessing unseen text for known participants; evaluating new participants on familiar stimuli addresses another distinct question. Neither establishes joint generalization, but neither is automatically an invalid evaluation. Claims that all existing methods suffer leakage should be qualified by their intended generalization targets.

Section 5.2 does not establish the claimed causal mechanisms. Decreasing validation loss or improving test scores with additional training is not itself evidence of overfitting. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together, while different splits also change training data and evaluation difficulty. Matched comparisons and shuffled-signal or no-signal controls are needed to distinguish memorization, distribution shift, and actual use of brain information. A randomly initialized but subsequently trained encoder does not establish that the encoder contributes little.

The claims of maximizing data utilization and improving generalization lack direct support. No retained/discarded sample counts or retention comparison with a simpler partitioning baseline are provided. Extending a fixed partition does not establish maximum retention, and adopting a stricter evaluation protocol does not itself demonstrate improved model generalization.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for the claimed released benchmark. The manuscript supplies some hyperparameters but no repository or split manifests, exact retained subject/story/sample counts, or sufficiently explicit inference settings, including whether reference prefixes are supplied during evaluation. Generation results lack variability estimates; the four reported seeds concern overlap measurements only. Corrected algorithms and metrics, reproducible splits, and controlled reruns are needed before a sound Findings recommendation, motivating resubmission next cycle.
